The Case for Privatizing Marriage: Why the State Should Exit the Wedding Business

Introduction

For centuries, the institution of marriage has occupied a peculiar position in liberal democracies—simultaneously regarded as the most intimate of personal commitments and as a heavily regulated state institution laden with legal privileges, obligations, and exclusions. This arrangement, inherited from an era when church and state were intertwined and women were legally subsumed into their husbands' identities, has persisted largely unexamined. Yet a growing chorus of voices from across the political spectrum—libertarians, feminists, legal scholars, and civil rights advocates—has begun questioning a fundamental premise: should the state be involved in marriage at all?

This essay argues that marriage should be entirely removed from the legal sphere. The state should cease issuing marriage licenses, abolish the legal category of marriage, and allow individuals to structure their domestic arrangements through private contracts and other existing legal mechanisms. Far from undermining family life or social stability, this reform would enhance individual liberty, promote genuine equality, separate religious from civil concerns, and create a more honest and flexible framework for the diverse forms of human commitment that characterize contemporary society.

Part I: The Historical Case—Marriage as an Artifact of Patriarchy and State Control

The Origins of State-Controlled Marriage

Understanding why the state should exit marriage requires understanding how it entered in the first place. State involvement in marriage did not arise from benevolent concern for romantic partnerships but from specific historical imperatives of control, property management, and social regulation.

In ancient Rome, marriage was primarily a private family matter, with the paterfamilias exercising control over household arrangements. The state's interest was largely confined to citizenship and inheritance questions among elites. Medieval canon law brought marriage under ecclesiastical jurisdiction, where the Church used it as an instrument of moral regulation and social control.

The modern system of state-licensed marriage emerged in the Protestant Reformation and subsequent centuries as governments wrested control from religious authorities. England's 1753 Marriage Act, requiring official registration and specific ceremonies, was explicitly designed to prevent clandestine marriages that circumvented parental authority and property arrangements. In the American colonies and early republic, marriage licensing served to prevent interracial unions, control the marriages of enslaved people, and enforce patriarchal family structures.

Marriage as Property Arrangement

The legal structure of marriage was, until remarkably recently, explicitly organized around the concept of coverture—the legal fiction that husband and wife were one person, and that person was the husband. Women lost their legal identity upon marriage, surrendering property rights, the ability to enter contracts, and legal standing in their own right.

While coverture has been formally abolished, the legal scaffolding of marriage still bears its imprint. The default rules governing marital property, the presumptions about domestic arrangements, and the difficulty of modifying standard marital terms through prenuptial agreements all reflect assumptions about unified household economics that trace back to patriarchal origins.

If marriage as a legal institution was designed for purposes—controlling women's sexuality, managing property transmission through male lines, preventing interracial mixing—that we now rightly reject, why do we assume the institution itself, once reformed, becomes neutral or beneficial? A vehicle designed for subjugation does not become an instrument of liberation simply by adding new passengers.

The Persistent Role of Exclusion

State marriage has always been fundamentally about exclusion—determining which relationships receive recognition and benefits while others are stigmatized or ignored. The history of marriage is a history of drawing lines: between races, between religions, between classes, and until recently, between sexualities.

The 1967 Loving v. Virginia decision struck down anti-miscegenation laws only 58 years ago—within living memory. The 2015 Obergefell v. Hodges decision extended marriage rights to same-sex couples barely a decade ago. In both cases, the fundamental harm was the state using marriage as a tool of exclusion, designating certain relationships as worthy and others as deviant.

The solution to discriminatory state marriage is not perfect state marriage—a goal that has proved elusive across centuries—but rather removing the state from the business of categorizing and hierarchically ranking intimate relationships altogether.

Part II: The Philosophical Case—Marriage Privatization and Liberal Principles

The Problem of State Endorsement

Liberal political philosophy, from Locke through Rawls, has grappled with the problem of state neutrality regarding competing conceptions of the good life. The state, in this tradition, should not endorse particular religious doctrines, lifestyle choices, or visions of human flourishing. It should instead provide a neutral framework within which individuals can pursue their own values.

State-recognized marriage flagrantly violates this principle. When the government issues marriage licenses, conducts ceremonies through state officials, and attaches a vast network of privileges to marital status, it sends an unmistakable message: this form of relationship is officially approved; others are inferior.

This endorsement function cannot be eliminated simply by expanding who may marry. Even after Obergefell, the state continues to privilege dyadic relationships over other forms of mutual commitment. It continues to favor romantic/sexual partnerships over deep friendships. It continues to assume that the proper unit of adult social organization is the couple rather than extended families, chosen families, or communities.

The argument that marriage should be expanded to include more relationships, while progressive in intent, still accepts the premise that the state should be in the business of officially approving some relationships over others. The logical extension of marriage equality is not infinite expansion of marriage but rather the recognition that state endorsement of intimate relationships is itself the problem.

Religious Freedom and Secular Government

The marriage debate has often been framed as a conflict between religious values and civil equality. This framing obscures a deeper truth: state involvement in marriage inherently entangles civil and religious functions in ways that should trouble both religious traditionalists and secularists.

For religious communities, marriage carries profound spiritual significance that varies dramatically across traditions. A Catholic understanding of marriage as an indissoluble sacrament differs fundamentally from a secular view of marriage as dissolvable civil contract, which differs again from various Protestant, Jewish, Islamic, Hindu, and other religious conceptions. By maintaining a single legal institution called "marriage," the state inevitably imposes one understanding on communities that hold different views.

When the state changed its definition of marriage to include same-sex couples, traditional religious communities experienced this as government redefinition of a sacred institution—not because they were necessarily correct about what marriage "really is," but because government monopolization of the marriage category meant that changes in civil marriage inevitably affected the social meaning of religious marriage as well.

Privatizing marriage would actually better serve religious freedom. Religious communities could define marriage according to their beliefs without worrying about state imposition, while those who reject religious frameworks could formalize their relationships without being forced into an institution laden with religious connotations. Marriage would mean what each community or couple determines it to mean rather than what the state decrees.

The Incoherence of "Marriage" as Legal Category

Modern marriage has become a legal grab-bag—a single category that bundles together hundreds of distinct legal rights, privileges, and obligations that have little logical connection to one another.

Consider the range of legal effects that attach to marriage in the United States:

  • Tax filing status and various tax benefits
  • Immigration sponsorship rights
  • Social Security survivor benefits
  • Presumption of paternity for children
  • Hospital visitation and medical decision-making authority
  • Inheritance rights in the absence of a will
  • Privilege against testifying against one's spouse in court
  • Property division rules upon divorce

The Case for Abolishing State Marriage: Why Government Should Exit the Bedroom Entirely

Introduction

Few institutions appear so natural, so permanent, and so obviously the proper province of law as marriage. Yet this appearance is deceptive. State-recognized marriage is a relatively recent, historically contingent, and philosophically unjustifiable arrangement that produces substantial harms — practical, political, and principled — while solving problems that alternative legal mechanisms would address more cleanly and fairly. The state has no compelling interest in designating some intimate relationships as officially legitimate while leaving others in legal shadow. The solution is not to expand marriage incrementally to new categories of couples, as important as that progress has been, but to remove the state from the marriage business entirely. Marriage should be what it was before governments claimed authority over it: a private commitment, a religious sacrament where desired, a social bond, or a contractual arrangement between adults — but not a legally privileged status conferred by the state.

This essay argues that case systematically. The argument proceeds through several pillars: the philosophical illegitimacy of state preference for particular relationship forms; the practical incoherence of the current system; the harms that state marriage produces; the availability of superior legal alternatives; and responses to the strongest objections. The goal is not to attack commitment, love, family, or community — it is to rescue those genuine goods from an unnecessary and distorting bureaucratic framework.

I. The Philosophical Foundation: Why the State Has No Business Designating Legitimate Relationships

The Autonomy Argument

Liberal political philosophy, from John Locke through John Stuart Mill to contemporary theorists like John Rawls, holds that the state's legitimate functions are constrained. The state may protect individuals from harm, enforce contracts, provide public goods, and maintain the infrastructure of a just society. What it may not legitimately do, in the liberal tradition, is impose a particular conception of the good life on citizens who have not consented to that conception and who harm no one by living differently.

Marriage, as currently constituted, is precisely such an imposition. When the state grants a bundle of approximately 1,100 federal legal rights and benefits — in the United States alone — exclusively to married couples, it is not merely enforcing private contracts. It is using law to declare that one particular relationship form is the preferred, legitimate, and governmentally endorsed way to organize intimate life. Citizens who choose cohabitation, polyamorous arrangements, close friendships, or deliberate singlehood are structurally disadvantaged not because their choices harm anyone but because they deviate from the state's preferred template.

This is a straightforward autonomy violation. Adults are sovereign over their own intimate lives. The state has no more business deciding that marriage is the correct way to organize intimate relationships than it has deciding that Protestantism is the correct religion, or that conservatism is the correct politics. The parallel to religious establishment is not merely rhetorical: for most of Western history, marriage was religious establishment, and civil marriage emerged partly as an attempt to disentangle the two. But partial disentanglement is not complete disentanglement.

The Neutrality Argument

Rawlsian political philosophy adds a related consideration. In a pluralist society, the state should justify its laws and policies using principles that reasonable citizens of diverse worldviews can accept — what Rawls called "public reason." Laws that rest on contested conceptions of human flourishing, religious doctrine, or particular cultural traditions fail this test.

State marriage fails it conspicuously. Different religious traditions, philosophical frameworks, and cultural communities hold radically different views about what marriage means, who should be able to marry, what obligations it creates, and how it should end. There is no neutral, publicly accessible reason why the state should endorse any particular version of this contested institution. The state can enforce contracts. The state can protect children. The state can facilitate inheritance and medical decision-making. None of these functions requires the state to pronounce that a relationship is legitimately "married."

The Dignity Argument

When the state recognizes some relationships and not others, it communicates a message about the relative legitimacy and dignity of those relationships. This message is not merely symbolic — it shapes culture, influences social attitudes, and has material consequences. Unmarried partners face practical indignities: being barred from hospital rooms, being treated as legal strangers in medical emergencies, being disadvantaged in immigration contexts, facing inheritance complications that married couples avoid automatically.

More fundamentally, the state's designation of "legitimate" and "illegitimate" relationships embeds a hierarchy of human worth into law. This is not an abstract concern. The history of state marriage regulation is substantially a history of exclusion: excluding same-sex couples, excluding interracial couples, treating women as legal appendages of their husbands, using marriage law as a tool of racial classification, denying marriage rights to enslaved people. The appropriate response to this history is not merely to expand who gets to enter the privileged category. It is to ask whether the state should be in the business of creating this hierarchy at all.

II. The Practical Case: State Marriage Is a Poorly Designed Legal Instrument

The Problem of Bundling

The most practically significant argument for marriage abolition is what legal scholars call the "bundling problem." State marriage combines an enormous range of legal consequences — property rights, inheritance, tax treatment, immigration status, medical decision-making authority, parental rights, spousal privilege in testimony, social security benefits, and dozens more — into a single all-or-nothing package.

This bundling is extraordinarily crude. It forces every couple to accept or reject an enormous standardized contract without being able to customize it to their actual circumstances and preferences. A couple that wants inheritance rights but not joint tax filing, or medical decision-making authority but not spousal immigration benefits, has no legal mechanism to achieve that combination within the marriage framework. They must take the bundle or leave it.

The bundling also creates perverse incentives. People marry for legal benefits they need — immigration status, health insurance access, inheritance protection — rather than because marriage reflects their actual relationship preferences. This distorts both the institution and the decisions of real people. The solution is disaggregation: making each bundle of rights available through separate, targeted legal instruments.

The One-Size-Fits-All Problem

State marriage law is designed for a particular relationship template: two adults, sexually exclusive, sharing a household, with an indefinite commitment, intending (presumptively) to have children. This template never described all marriages accurately, but it described the modal marriage in a particular historical and cultural context. Today it describes an increasingly small minority of actual intimate arrangements.

The demographic reality of contemporary life includes: long-term cohabiting couples who choose not to marry; polyamorous families with multiple committed partners; close-knit friendships that involve deep commitment and mutual dependence without romantic or sexual dimensions; elderly people who want to combine households and finances without formally remarrying; same-sex couples, whether or not they choose marriage; and individuals who choose deliberate singlehood without thereby forswearing all intimate commitments.

State marriage law cannot accommodate this diversity without endless exceptions, extensions, and complications. Every expansion of marriage rights to new categories of couples reveals, rather than resolves, the fundamental problem: the state is trying to impose a single legal template on an irreducibly diverse range of human relationships. Abolition, combined with flexible alternative legal instruments, is the only solution that actually respects this diversity.

The Tax Code Absurdity

The interaction of marriage with tax law alone illustrates the incoherence of state marriage as policy. The United States tax code simultaneously creates "marriage penalties" — situations where two people pay more tax married than they would as singles — and "marriage bonuses" — situations where they pay less. These effects are arbitrary from the perspective of tax policy; they are artifacts of grafting a complex tax system onto a marital status category that was never designed with tax efficiency in mind.

Why should a couple's income tax liability depend on whether they have performed a marriage ceremony? There is no coherent tax policy justification for this. It is simply a consequence of having bundled tax treatment into marriage status. Disaggregation would allow tax policy to be designed on its own terms, based on actual household economics, without reference to relationship status.

The Social Security Problem

Similar absurdities pervade Social Security. Spousal and survivor benefits were designed in the 1930s for a world in which married women typically did not work outside the home and depended financially on their husbands. Today, these benefits create substantial inequities: a single person who works and pays Social Security taxes throughout their life receives far less in expected lifetime benefits than a married person with a non-working or low-earning spouse, even if they have identical earnings records.

This is not merely unfair to single people. It is an enormous implicit subsidy to a particular household arrangement, paid for by everyone. The justification, such as it was, has largely disappeared as women's labor force participation has equalized. The Social Security system would be fairer, more sustainable, and more coherent if it were redesigned around individuals' actual earnings and contributions rather than around their marital status.

III. The Harms Produced by State Marriage

Harms to Those Outside the Institution

The most direct harms of state marriage fall on those excluded from it. Despite the legalization of same-sex marriage in many jurisdictions, the basic problem remains: state marriage creates a two-tier system of intimate relationships, and those in the second tier bear real costs.

Non-married cohabiting partners — a category that includes many people who have made deep mutual commitments — lack automatic legal protections. When one partner is hospitalized, the other may have no right to information or to participate in medical decisions. When a partner dies without a will, the survivor may inherit nothing under intestacy laws that automatically favor blood relatives. When a cohabiting relationship ends, there is often no legal framework for equitable distribution of shared assets. These are serious, concrete harms imposed on real people who have harmed no one.

The response, "they should just get married," is both practically inadequate and philosophically unacceptable. It is practically inadequate because not everyone can or wants to marry: some people are already legally married to someone else, some are in relationships that include more than two people, some object to state involvement in their intimate lives for reasons of principle, and some simply do not want to take a step their partner is not ready for. It is philosophically unacceptable because it amounts to saying: conform to our preferred relationship form, or forgo legal protection. This is precisely the coercive pressure that autonomy-respecting government must not impose.

Harms Within the Institution

State marriage also produces harms for those inside it. The bundling of legal consequences into marriage creates a mechanism for control and coercion within relationships. In abusive relationships, the legal and financial entanglements of marriage can make leaving extremely difficult: joint property, shared debts, complex divorce proceedings, immigration status dependent on an abusive spouse's cooperation.

Divorce law, despite improvements, remains in many jurisdictions a terrain of adversarial conflict that imposes enormous financial and psychological costs on divorcing couples and, most importantly, on their children. The state's involvement in intimate relationships does not end when relationships end; it simply changes character, often becoming a vehicle for protracted legal warfare. The privatization of relationship formation and dissolution would not eliminate all conflict — human beings in disagreement will find ways to dispute — but it would remove the overlay of state-administered adversarial process that amplifies and prolongs conflict.

The Distributive Justice Problem

State marriage, combined with means-tested benefit programs, creates deeply perverse incentives for poor people. The "marriage penalty" in the context of means-tested benefits — Medicaid, food stamps, housing assistance — can be severe: two poor people who marry may lose eligibility for benefits that they received as individuals, leaving them worse off than if they had remained legally single while living together. This is not a minor tax code wrinkle; it is a substantial disincentive to marriage imposed primarily on the poorest Americans.

The policy simultaneously fails on its own terms: if policymakers believe marriage is beneficial, why does the policy structure penalize poor people for marrying? And it fails from a basic justice perspective: why should intimate life decisions have major consequences for access to basic necessities? The answer to both questions is the same: because marriage has been inappropriately bundled into systems of social provision. Designing social provision around actual household economics and individual need, rather than marital status, would be both fairer and more coherent.

Harms to Religious Liberty

Counterintuitively, state marriage harms religious liberty — for religious people as well as non-religious people. When the state creates a legal institution called "marriage," it creates inevitable conflict between the state's definition of that institution and religious communities' definitions of it. This conflict is not merely theoretical: it has generated genuine legal disputes about whether religious institutions can refuse to perform marriages that violate their doctrines, whether religious businesses must serve same-sex couples, and how to balance competing claims of conscience and equality.

These conflicts arise precisely because the state has claimed the word "marriage" and attached legal consequences to it. If the state were to exit the marriage business — registering "civil unions" or "domestic partnerships" as functional contracts while leaving "marriage" to religious and cultural communities to define as they see fit — the conflict would largely dissolve. Religious communities would be free to define marriage according to their traditions without any implication for civil law. No one's religious ceremonies would be required to be legally valid, and no one's legally valid partnership would need to be religiously blessed. This complete separation, rather than the awkward current compromise, best protects both civil equality and religious freedom.

IV. The Alternative: A Better Legal Framework

Abolishing state marriage does not mean abolishing legal protections for intimate relationships. Abolishing State-Regulated Marriage: The Case for Complete Legal Separation

For centuries, marriage has existed both as a deeply personal relationship and as a legally regulated institution. I. Marriage Is a Personal, Not Political, Relationship

At its core, marriage is a voluntary bond between individuals. For some, it is a religious sacrament; for others, a purely emotional commitment; still for others, a social or cultural tradition. None of these dimensions require political oversight. Government involvement in marriage assumes that the state has the moral authority to validate, regulate, and even dissolve intimate relationships. But such authority is unjustifiable — after all, the state does not issue licenses for friendship, nor does it regulate the emotional bonds of parent-child relationships beyond essential protections against harm.

By privatizing marriage — treating it as a personal agreement between consenting adults — the bond would be a matter of free association, just like any other private contractual or religious arrangement. II. State-Defined Marriage Creates Inequality by Design

Contrary to the belief that legal marriage promotes fairness, the structure of state-defined marriage artificially privileges a certain type of relationship at the expense of others. Married couples often receive special tax benefits, inheritance rights, immigration opportunities, and healthcare decision-making powers unavailable to unmarried individuals, no matter the longevity or seriousness of their relationships. This creates a two-tiered system where the government rewards one specific model of family or partnership while ignoring — or actively disadvantaging — alternatives.

Private contractual agreements could provide all necessary legal mechanisms for rights such as hospital visitation, inheritance, and shared property ownership, without the state reserving such privileges for only those who meet its definition of “married.” Abolishing state-recognized marriage would thus eliminate legal favoritism and allow all relationships to be treated equitably, regardless of form.

III. Removing Marriage From Law Would Reduce Cultural Conflict

Much of the public divisiveness over marriage law — especially in recent decades — has stemmed from the fact that the state acts as the arbiter of which relationships are legitimate. Conflicts over whether same-sex couples, plural unions, or non-traditional arrangements should be legally recognized arise precisely because legal recognition is exclusive. If the state were completely uninvolved, political disputes over “who can marry” would vanish, because there would be no state license to fight over.

By privatizing marriage, debates about legitimacy would shift from political arenas to cultural, religious, or personal contexts, where individuals could freely associate with communities sharing their values without imposing their definitions on others via state power.

IV. Historical Justifications Are No Longer Relevant

Historically, marriage law served practical governance purposes: consolidating property, ensuring paternal certainty in an era before DNA testing, regulating succession and inheritance, and securing alliances. But modern legal and technological systems make these purposes obsolete.

Property law, inheritance law, and parental rights statutes already function without requiring marriage as a prerequisite — and when they still do, it is due to outdated legal frameworks that could easily be reformed. Child custody determinations are handled through family law regardless of marital status; wills and trusts handle inheritance without a marriage license; and advanced reproductive testing removes the need for the presumption of paternity embedded in marriage law. One common concern is that eliminating legal marriage would create uncertainty in cases of divorce, property division, and shared financial obligations. Yet contract law already provides all the tools necessary for handling such matters. Couples, friends, or families could draft relationship contracts specifying financial arrangements, support obligations, or guardianship agreements. These could be as detailed or as simple as the parties desire, tailored to their unique circumstances rather than bound by a one-size-fits-all state marriage code.

If conflicts arise, mediation and the courts could enforce such agreements precisely as they would with any other contract — without state-by-default imposition of marriage-specific obligations that may not reflect the intentions of the individuals involved.

VI. The Moral and Philosophical Argument for Non-Interference

At its heart, this is about autonomy. A free society respects the right of individuals to define their own relationships, provided they do not infringe upon the rights of others. Government involvement in marriage assumes a paternalistic role: implying citizens need official validation for their personal commitments. This runs directly counter to the principles of individual liberty, bodily autonomy, and free association.

The state’s interest should be limited to protecting individuals from harm and enforcing agreements voluntarily entered into — not prescribing the form or content of personal relationships.

Conclusion: Freedom Through Separation

The complete abolition of state recognition and regulation of marriage would liberate human relationships from political control, dismantle legal favoritism, remove perennial cultural conflicts, and reinforce individual liberty. In a society built on the principles of equality and freedom, there is no place for government-sanctioned intimacy.

By treating marriage entirely as a private matter — whether religious, secular, polyamorous, monogamous, or otherwise — we can create a society in which individuals are free to form partnerships that reflect their own values, negotiate their own terms, and live without state intrusion in the most personal areas of their lives. It’s time to remove marriage from the law books and return it to where it belongs: to the people themselves.

The Unshackled Union: Why the State Should Exit the Marriage Business

For centuries, the institution of marriage has been entwined with the power and authority of the state, creating a legal framework that defines, regulates, and sanctions one of humanity’s most intimate human bonds. This entanglement, however, is neither natural nor necessary. It is a historical artifact, a vestige of an era when personal lives were considered public property. The time has come for a radical, yet deeply principled, reformation: the complete abolition of state recognition and regulation of marriage. Marriage should be dismantled as a legal category and restored to its rightful domain as a private commitment, a personal promise, or a customizable civil contract, entirely outside the jurisdiction of the state.

I. The Historical and Philosophical Foundations of State Marriage Are Obsolete

The state’s historical role in marriage was born not of concern for love or partnership, but of power and control. Its functions were threefold: to legitimize heirs for stable inheritance (a concern of property and aristocracy), to regulate sexual morality and procreation for societal order, and to create a clear, taxable unit for census and resource allocation. This framework, rooted in patriarchal structures and social engineering, has no place in a modern society that values individual autonomy over collective conformity.

Philosophically, the liberal state exists to protect individual rights—life, liberty, and property—while leaving the realm of personal choice and morality to the conscience of the individual. By issuing marriage licenses and setting conditions (age, capacity, prohibitions on bigamy), the state oversteps its proper boundary. It transforms a deeply personal vow into a government-granted privilege, creating a hierarchy of relationships where those outside the state’s definition are deemed "less than." Why should the state have the authority to decide which loving, consenting adult relationships are worthy of its seal of approval? This is not protection; it is paternalism.

II. State Regulation Creates Injustice and Exclusion

The state’s marriage regime is inherently exclusionary and often unjust. By creating a singular, legal definition, it inevitably marginalizes those who do not fit its template—whether by choice or circumstance. Polyamorous relationships, platonic life partners, and other complex human arrangements are denied the legal protections and social recognition afforded to the "traditional" couple. This is not a failure of these relationships, but a failure of the state’s rigid, one-size-fits-all model.

Furthermore, the state’s entanglement creates legal traps. Divorce proceedings, often adversarial and financially ruinous, are a direct product of dissolving a state-licensed contract. The state’s courts become arbiters of personal failings, a role for which they are ill-suited and which causes immense suffering. A private contract, negotiated with terms relevant to the specific couple (including fair exit clauses), could achieve the same goals of clarity and protection without the state’s destructive intervention in a private dissolution.

III. A Better Path: Voluntary Private Contracts and Social Recognition

Abolishing state marriage does not mean abandoning legal protections for families. Instead, it liberates individuals to design their own legal arrangements through private law. Couples and families could use existing contract law, trust law, and wills to establish the rights and responsibilities they find meaningful. This could cover:

  • Property and Assets: Agreeing on ownership, division, and inheritance.
  • Medical and End-of-Life Decisions: Granting powers of attorney and healthcare proxy.
  • Child-Rearing Arrangements: Clearly defining rights, responsibilities, and support (though the state’s role in child protection would remain separate).
  • Family Benefits: Corporations and organizations could, and often already do, recognize domestic partnerships or designates beneficiaries based on an employee’s own contract, not a government license.

This approach is vastly more flexible and equitable. It empowers people rather than pigeonholing them. It treats adults as competent agents capable of defining their own relationships, rather than as subjects requiring state sanction for their intimate choices.

IV. Addressing Counterarguments: Protection and Tradition

Opponents will argue that this would undermine protections for spouses and children. This is a misunderstanding. Protections would not disappear; they would be privatized and, in many cases, become more precise. The state’s role would refocus on its legitimate duties: enforcing voluntary contracts, protecting children from harm (via child welfare laws, not marriage law), and ensuring fair treatment in cases of dispute.

Others will claim the state must uphold the "sanctity of marriage" or a particular cultural tradition. The state is not, and should not be, a guardian of any particular religious or cultural doctrine. To use government power to enshrine one tradition’s view of a sacred union is to coerce those of other beliefs. True respect for tradition is found in voluntary practice, not in law. Individuals are free to marry in their church, mosque, or temple, but that ceremony should carry no more legal weight than any other private promise unless they separately choose to draft a private contract.

Conclusion: Freedom as the Highest Social Value

The institution of state-recognized marriage is a relic. It is a tool of control masquerading as a source of protection. Its continued existence unnecessarily inserts the bureaucracy of the state into the most personal corners of human life, creating inequality, complexity, and conflict where there need be none.

To abolish state marriage is not to diminish love or commitment. On the contrary, it elevates them. It declares that a promise between people is so profound that it does not require a government permit to be valid. It trusts individuals to define their own relationships and to arrange their legal and financial affairs through voluntary, private instruments. It separates the spiritual and personal from the legal and procedural, allowing each to flourish in its proper sphere.

The state should be a neutral referee, not a gatekeeper of the heart. It should enforce the contracts we make and protect the vulnerable among us, but it must leave the sacred and the private to us. In removing marriage from the law, we do not destroy it; we free it. We move from an era of sanctioned relationships to an era of chosen ones, where the only authority that matters is the one born of mutual respect, love, and freely given commitment.
